novel_actions_proposed.label: separate_then_assess_professionally
novel_actions_proposed.description: Immediately separate the child from the dog as a safety measure, then pursue professional veterinary and behavioral assessment to identify treatable causes and develop a humane management plan.

novel_actions_proposed.label: separate_then_assess_professionally
novel_actions_proposed.description: Remove the child from the dog's environment while the cause of aggression is investigated, ensuring no one in the household (including caregivers) is used as an experiment environment during the assessment period.

novel_actions_proposed.label: separate_then_assess_professionally
novel_actions_proposed.description: Implement strict physical separation as immediate risk control, then engage a veterinarian and qualified behaviorist to diagnose underlying causes (pain, fear, resource guarding) before any corrective intervention is attempted.

points_of_disagreement: The degree to which 'separation' implies permanent rehoming versus temporary management was left partially unresolved, with the advisor most explicitly framing it as non-permanent.
The role and risk exposure of third-party caregivers (babysitter/neighbor) in the interim period was raised primarily by the Affected Third Party and not fully addressed by the other agents.

The extent to which the dog's welfare and chance of rehabilitation should weigh against the urgency of child safety was emphasized differently across agents, with the advisor placing more weight on humane dog outcomes.
summary: All three agents converged on a novel action that goes beyond the original binary options: immediately separate the child from the dog as a non-negotiable safety measure, and then pursue professional veterinary and behavioral assessment to identify treatable root causes before any corrective intervention. None of the agents endorsed leaving the child in contact with the dog during a correction attempt, and none endorsed immediate permanent separation without first seeking professional diagnosis. The primary disagreements were matters of emphasis—how much weight to give the dog's welfare and rehabilitation prospects, how to protect third-party caregivers during the interim, and whether 'separation' is temporary or permanent—but these did not undermine the shared directional consensus.
